articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Marco Rubio’s second visit to India this year yielded little in terms of results

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India must adopt a pro-active position in the Saudi-Houthi conflict

The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Core sector data indicate impending growth slowdowns

The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Domestic manufacturing and foreign partnerships must go hand-in-hand

The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Economic objectives can be met only in a stable security environment

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The FSSAI must expand restrictions to cover all added sugars in infant foods

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: GBA invites designs to improve Bengaluru’s public spaces
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The initiative, Bengaluru Design: Open Call, under Bengaluru Jatre, is open to designers, architects, artists, students and other creative thinkers

The Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) has invited citizens to submit design ideas to improve Bengaluru’s everyday public spaces, including bus stops, streetlights, public benches, road medians, waste bins, shopfronts and neighbourhood identities.

The initiative, Bengaluru Design: Open Call, under Bengaluru Jatre, is open to designers, architects, artists, students and other creative thinkers. Submissions will close on November 15. Shortlisted designs will be showcased during Bengaluru Jatre, scheduled from December 4 to 13. The best proposals will be selected by a jury constituted by the GBA.

Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda said the initiative aims to connect citizens’ creativity with the city’s everyday needs. “A city is experienced not just through its major infrastructure but through the everyday spaces people use. We want citizens to bring forward ideas that make Bengaluru more accessible, welcoming and liveable,” he said.

The design challenges include improving street lighting, providing better shelter and accessibility at bus stops, making public seating more comfortable, redesigning waste bins and civic signboards, and developing neighbourhood identities that reflect local history and culture. Participants can also propose integrated improvements to a 500-metre stretch, incorporating pedestrian movement, road crossings, greenery, lighting, public transport, accessibility and safety. Another challenge invites ideas for developing distinct visual identities for Bengaluru’s five city corporations under the GBA.

The authority said proposals should be practical, affordable, inclusive and scalable, keeping in mind maintenance requirements, existing infrastructure, available materials and the operational needs of civic agencies.

“Good design must go beyond how something looks. It must work on the ground, be affordable to maintain, improve people’s everyday experience and be practical for our civic agencies to take forward,” Mr. Gowda said.

Selected proposals will be shared with the relevant city corporations for consideration and possible implementation, subject to feasibility in terms of technical, financial, operational and site-specific aspects. Entries can be sent to support@bengalurujatre.in by November 15.

articles.title: Kadapa police to seek cancellation of TDP spokesperson’s gun licence after alleged firing in Nandalur
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Both Tirupati and Kadapa police are equally at a loss as to how to deal with a weapon that, although licensed, has not been mentioned in the official records

Shots allegedly fired into the air by a Telugu Desam Party (TDP) leader during a clash in the nomination phase for the ZPTC and MPTC elections in Nandalur mandal of Kadapa district on October 22 (Thursday) have left the TDP in a piquant situation and the ruling NDA embarrassed.

TDP spokesperson Koduru Balasubramanyam, a Tirupati-based medical professional, reportedly fired several rounds in the air when members of his group clashed with a rival gang led by Yeddula Sagar during the nomination phase on Thursday.

The Rajampet sub-divisional police rushed to the spot and brought the situation under control. They seized the weapon and arrested eight persons involved in the melee. Mr. Balasubramanyam was admitted to a hospital, citing a rib fracture.

Though licensed weapons have to be deposited with the police when the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) comes into effect, the TDP leader has apparently kept the department guessing by carrying it to a troublesome spot.

Mr. Balasubramanyam had actually obtained the licence following due procedure from the Tirupati District Collector, citing security reasons, and purchased a weapon. However, the procedure mandates the person to share details of the weapon with the Collectorate, which will have to be recorded and then passed on to the police department for further monitoring.
In this case, Mr. Balasubramanyam had failed to complete the latter part. Since the procedure has not been taken to its logical end, the department is completely in the dark over his weapon.

“A total of 550 weapon licenses have been issued in Tirupati district, of which all but 29 have been surrendered ahead of the nomination phase. Our people are following up to obtain the remaining weapons soon. We will not insist upon surrendering the 89 licensed weapons issued to bankers for security purposes (shifting of cash, guarding lockers, among others),” Superintendent of Police (Tirupati) L. Subbarayudu said.

Since Mr. Balasubramanyam had not informed the Tirupati Collectorate about his weapon, the district police were understandably clueless about it, and as a result, reportedly did not demand its surrender.
After the incident, the Kadapa police were equally at a loss as to how to deal with a weapon that, although licensed, had not been mentioned in the official records.

“The weapon meant for use in self-defence was apparently used without any provocation. We will write to the appropriate authority to seek cancellation of the license,” Superintendent of Police (Kadapa) Nachiket Vishwanath Shelke told The Hindu.
Meanwhile, the TDP, which has been claiming an incident-free nomination phase, is on the defensive because the incident involves its own official spokesperson

articles.title: Blood of youths at Jantar Mantar cries out for justice, says writer Sarah Joseph
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Writer inaugurates AISF’s day-and-night sit-in in Thrissur, alleging attacks on democratic rights and calling for nationwide protests against the suppression of student movements

The blood of youths shed at protest sites at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi was crying out for justice, writer Sarah Joseph said, calling for a nationwide resistance against the alleged suppression of democratic rights and constitutional values. She was addressing a 24-hour satyagraha organised by the All India Students’ Federation (AISF) Thrissur district committee on Pattalam Road in Thrissur from Saturday evening (October 24, 2026).

Political equality, democracy and constitutional values had been undermined under the RSS-led dispensation, she alleged. Students and youth across the country were being forced to take to the streets to assert even their right to uphold the national flag, she said, accusing the authorities of deliberately creating conditions to disrupt such protests.

Ms. Joseph alleged that RSS activists were being brought into protest venues to target women and girl students, indulging even in sexual harassment. Left student and youth organisations, along with other groups, were conducting peaceful protests in the national capital following Gandhian principles, but attempts were being made behind the scenes to suppress and sabotage their agitations, she said. “There must be a strong public outcry against this. Every part of the country must turn into a Jantar Mantar,” she said.

Describing the developments in Delhi as a blatant violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, Ms. Joseph alleged that the government was deploying its repressive machinery to prevent dissent from emerging on the streets. The Modi government would eventually have to bow before the fighting spirit of students and young people, she said. The younger generation, which was taking to the streets without waiting for calls to action and demonstrating a strong democratic consciousness, offered hope for the future, she added.

Repeated attempts at repression were only making society more fearless, she said, warning the government against underestimating the role of young people in protecting Indian democracy. The satyagraha began with a percussion performance led by Kalamandalam Ranju Panjal and his troupe. Poet Engandiyur Chandrasekharan recited his poem ‘Theeppattu’.

CPI national council member and MLA K. Rajan, artist K.G. Babu and AISF district secretary Mithun Pottakkaran addressed the gathering. AISF district vice-president Alan Paul Varghese presided over the function. CPI national executive member K.P. Rajendran, State Secretariat member and MLA K.K. Valsaraj, State executive members V.S. Sunilkumar and Rajaji Mathew Thomas, senior CPI leader C.N. Jayadevan, district secretary K.G. Sivanandan, AIYF general secretary Dinesh Seerangara, and several leaders of mass organisations attended the event.

Representatives of AITUC, the Kerala Mahila Sangham, AIYF, the BKMU, the Pravasi Federation, the KGOF and Yuvakala Sahithi held rallies in solidarity with the protesters. Songs and protest anthems were performed under the leadership of Yuvakala Sahithi district secretary Soman Thamarakkulam. Cultural programmes were also presented. Poet Engandiyur Chandrasekharan lit the cultural solidarity flame organised by Yuvakala Sahithi at the venue. The 24-hour satyagraha concluded on Sunday with the hoisting of the national flag.

articles.title: Health Department gears up for cyclone, identifies 26,000 pregnant women
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Officials told to ensure uninterrupted emergency services, shift expectant mothers in vulnerable areas to safer locations
Health Minister Satya Kumar Yadav has directed officials to ensure uninterrupted emergency healthcare services in areas likely to be affected by the approaching cyclonic storm.

On Sunday (October 25), he reviewed the Health and Family Welfare Department’s preparedness in view of the red alerts issued for several districts on October 27 and 28, as the State braces for the ‘Very Severe Cyclonic Storm’.

According to a department release, Mr. Yadav stressed the need to maintain an uninterrupted supply of medicines at government healthcare facilities in low-lying areas. He also directed officials to shift pregnant women whose expected delivery dates fall between October 23 and November 6 to safer locations.

The department has identified more than 26,000 pregnant women living in flood-prone areas and those with health complications for admission to hospitals. Arrangements are also being made to shift pregnant women from areas with no transport facilities.

Health and Family Welfare Commissioner K.V.N. Chakradhar Babu has directed all District Medical and Health Officers to ensure adequate stocks of essential medicines, oral rehydration solution (ORS), intravenous saline, maternity medicines, newborn care supplies, oxygen, generators, fuel and drinking water.

Health Minister Satya Kumar Yadav has directed officials to ensure uninterrupted emergency healthcare services in areas likely to be affected by the approaching cyclonic storm.

According to a department release, Mr. Yadav stressed the need to maintain an uninterrupted supply of medicines at government healthcare facilities in low-lying areas. He also directed officials to shift pregnant women whose expected delivery dates fall between October 23 and November 6 to safer locations.

The department has identified more than 26,000 pregnant women living in flood-prone areas and those with health complications for admission to hospitals. Arrangements are also being made to shift pregnant women from areas with no transport facilities.

Health and Family Welfare Commissioner K.V.N. Chakradhar Babu has directed all District Medical and Health Officers to ensure adequate stocks of essential medicines, oral rehydration solution (ORS), intravenous saline, maternity medicines, newborn care supplies, oxygen, generators, fuel and drinking water.

Frontline health workers have been asked to identify families with pregnant women, postpartum mothers, newborns, young children, elderly people, persons with disabilities and those requiring regular medication.

Officials have also been directed to ensure proper sanitation and access to safe drinking water in affected villages, and remain vigilant against any unusual rise in infectious diseases.

articles.title: Chef Damu passes away at 72
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: In 2010, Chef Damu entered the Guinness Book of World Records by cooking 617 dishes in 24 hours. He, a recipient of Padma Shri, was one of the judges on the popular television series ‘Cooku With Comali’.

Chef K. Damodaran popularly called ‘Chef Damu ’, whose simple yet delicious recipes enlivened thousands of kitchens, passed away in Chennai on Sunday (October 25, 2026) after brief illness. He was 72 and is survived by wife Usha and daughter Akshaya, a doctor, working in London. According to family sources, his last rites would be held at 3 p.m. on Monday.

Born in September 1954 in West Mambalam to Kothandaraman who worked at the Secretariat and Kothainayaki, a homemaker, he was interested in cooking from a very young age and wanted to take up catering as a career.

The first Indian chef to receive a doctorate in hotel management and catering technology, he started his career in the Tamil Nadu Tourism Development Corporation (TTDC) as a management trainee in 1977 after completing Diploma in Hotel management and Catering Technology from Institute of Hotel Management, Taramani, Chennai. He then completed B.Com and obtained an MBA too.

In December 2010, he entered the Guinness Book of World Records for the Longest Cooking Marathon — Individual after he set the record by cooking 617 dishes (190 kg of food) in 24 hours, 30 minutes and 12 seconds.
Chef Damu holds the Guinness Book of World Records certificate in Chennai on December 22, 2010. | Photo Credit: S.R. Raghunathan

He has hosted cooking programmes on several channels and was one of the judges on the popular television series ‘Cooku With Comali’. He was passionate about Tamil Nadu food, especially Chettinad food. “He used to grind his own masalas and would tell us, his fans to do the same. I follow many of his recipes,” said S. Geetha, a homemaker in Anna Nagar.
(from left) Chefs Venkatesh Bhat and Damu in a promo still for ‘Cooku with Comali’ | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement
He was associated with the Government of Tamil Nadu in the implementation of mid-day (noon meal) meal scheme during 2008 and 2011 and the improved quality of food provided to school children.

Chef Venkatesh Bhat, said chef Damu, the first from the community of chefs to be awarded a Padma Shri (in 2025 ) in Tamil Nadu, was an inspiration for many youth to enter the hospitality industry and consider catering as a career. “He was a great human being. We have travelled together for 15 years. I cannot forget the days that we spent during the TV shoots. He was the president of the South Indian Culinary Academy.”
Chef Damu in Vellore in 2018 | Photo Credit: V.M. Maninathan

Musician Binny Krishnakumar, who has participated in ‘Cooku With Comali’ as a guest, recalled how her daughter, Sivangi had bonded so well with Damu. “He would treat her like his own daughter. He was great fun to be with. We will miss him.”
He was associated with The Hindu ’s ‘Our State Our Taste’ cookery competition as judge for several years.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The competing concerns highlight the challenge facing the ethanol procurement framework: balancing the availability and cost of different feedstocks.

The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Inflation in rural areas was found to be higher than in urban areas; headline CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities

High-frequency data collected by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for October (till 19th), suggest a broad-based increase in food prices, said RBI officials in the October edition of RBI Bulletin, which was released on Friday (October 23, 2026).

“Among cereals, rice and wheat prices continued to increase. Prices of major pulses also went up sequentially. Edible oil prices also recorded a slow and broad-based increase, led by mustard and palm oil,” they wrote in the ‘State of the Economy’ article.
Among vegetables, while potato prices declined and the pace of onion price increases dropped, tomato prices picked up, they added.

articles.title: IndusInd Bank posts profit of ₹1,242 crores in Q2; asset quality improvement and interest income drives growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago

IndusInd Bank Limited posted a net profit of ₹1,242 crore for the quarter ended September, up 20% sequentially and trimming net loss of ₹437 for the same quarter in the preceding year. The bank had incurred net loss for the same period in previous year due to an increase in microfinance provisioning and write-offs.

The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago. Sequentially, interest income declined by 2%. NII for half year (H1FY27) rose to ₹9,254, up 2.3% on year.

Asset quality of the bank improved substantially, with gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio at 2.73% compared to 3.60% on year and net NPA declining to 0.83% from 1.04% in Q2FY26. However, the net interest margin of the bank slipped to 3.23% from 3.32% a year ago.

Net revenue of the bank for the period rose to ₹6,817 crores compared to ₹6,00 crores a year. A decline in operating expenses also helped push the bottom-line numbers, with expenses slipping to ₹3,943 crores in July-Septemeber from ₹4,013 crore for the same period last year.
Deposits of the bank rose 10% year-on-year to ₹4.28 crores. Advances of the bank for the period stood at 3.63 crores.
IndusInd held provisions of $9,012 crore as of September 30, with the provision coverage ratio at 70%.

IndusInd Bank raised nearly $3.5 billion via the Reserve Bank of India’s special window for foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) account, which was impacted the contraction in NIM. The bank said recovery in margin related to FCNR-B is expected over the next two quarters.

“Q2 reflects the growing strength of the IndusInd Bank franchise and the progress we have made in rebuilding momentum across the business. Our Q2 results demonstrate that the growth has strengthened, profitability has improved, asset quality trends remain encouraging, and our funding profile is becoming more granular and resilient,” Rajiv Anand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of IndusInd Bank said.

The bank also informed the exchanges on Friday (October 23, 2026) that the Board of Directors of the lender has appointed Priyanka Sinha as an Additional Director in the category of Non-Executive Independent Director for a period of four consecutive years, till October 22, 2030.

Speaking to the media at post-earnings conference call, the bank said it remains confident of reaching a 1% exit return on assets for FY27. Bank also expects loans growth momentum to continue driven by retail and wholesale lending. Shares of IndusInd Bank Ltd closed at ₹835.00 on Friday, down 1.76%, on the BSE.

articles.title: Government to modify labour survey to capture gig economy, unpaid household workers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Periodic Labour Force Survey will include additional questions to measure labour underutilisation

The Union government has decided to change the design and structure of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to track digital platform workers and capture engagement in unpaid household, caregiving, volunteer, and trainee work. The PLFS will also include additional questions to measure labour underutilisation.

According to a press release and concept note issued in New Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026), the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), has proposed modifications to the PLFS sampling design starting January 2027. The survey schedule will also change.

A separate Second Stage Stratum (SSS) will be introduced in the PLFS to identify households with at least one digital platform worker. An additional entry will be added to the questionnaire to determine whether any member of the household has engaged in digital platform work during the specified reference period.

“There will be four SSSs in rural areas and five in urban areas, with 14 households canvassed in each selected First Stage Unit (FSU). This revision in SSS formation is expected to improve the coverage of digital platform workers and facilitate more comprehensive data collection on this emerging segment of the labour market,” the press release said.

According to the concept note, a large proportion of women in India spend considerable time on unpaid household and caregiving activities, such as cooking, cleaning, childcare, and caring for elderly, sick, or disabled family members. “While such activities contribute significantly to household well-being and facilitate the participation of other household members in paid employment, they have not been measured separately in PLFS until now,” it noted, adding that specific questions will be incorporated to capture engagement in own-use production of goods, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work, and unpaid trainee work.

Additionally, the criteria for sample allocation and stratification have been updated based on the experience of the previous two years. “These revisions are expected to improve the efficiency of sample allocation and stratification and ensure better representation of population variations, which in turn will minimise operational difficulties during sample selection,” the press release said.

articles.title: Crude oil sourcing presently volatile; procuring more on landed basis: HPCL Chief
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) informed the state-owned OMC is procuring more on landed basis than on FOB basis and term contracts

Crude oil sourcing at present is very volatile and unpredictable, and Hindustan Petroleum is procuring more on a delivered basis than free-on-board (FOB) and term contracts, Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) of the state-owned oil-marketing company told analysts in an investor call on Friday (October 23, 2026).
Purchases on delivered basis entail the seller bearing the cost of shipping the oil and associated risks until it reaches the buyer’s port or facility.

“All I can say if you look at crude premiums and landed cost: there are times when there are premiums and there are times when you can even pick it up at discounts. It is a very ‘Wild West’ right now” he said.
Separately, Mr. Kaushal also explained there could be instances of discount though the freights could be very high at that time.
Srividya Venkataraman, Director (Finance) informed analysts that freight costs had doubled between the first quarter and the second quarter.
She observed that shipping costs on a Suezmax tanker moved up to $9 per barrel from around $4 per barrel in June.
Though, Mr. Kaushal also stated that landed price may not be as high as it may appear.

“The producers of oil are also stuck. Thus, the astronomical freight rates that you see: if you strike a good deal, you can get is almost managed on the producer,” he explained, adding, “So, the net back to producers in many situations, especially those who are stuck or where there is stranded oil right now, the net backs are much lower than what is in the public domain.”

The HPCL chief also told analysts that the company is procuring more on landed basis expect in cases where sending a ship is cheaper. He added this is also to avert the probability of a ship being attacked enroute.
Ms. Venkataraman informed that under-recoveries on liquified petroleum gas (LPG) stood at ₹245 per cylinder in October and is projected at ₹327 per cylinder in November.
She added that the total under-recovery for LPG in the September-end quarter stood at ₹500 crores.

Separately, Mr. Kaushal also informed analysts that Hindustan Petroleum has petrol and diesel stocks combined for twenty days. This excludes the crude that is presently being processed in their refineries.

Srividya Venkataraman, Director (Finance) informed analysts that freight costs had doubled between the first quarter and the second quarter.

“The producers of oil are also stuck. Thus, the astronomical freight rates that you see: if you strike a good deal, you can get is almost managed on the producer,” he explained, adding, “So, the net back to producers in many situations, especially those who are stuck or where there is stranded oil right now, the net backs are much lower than what is in the public domain.”

Ms. Venkataraman informed that under-recoveries on liquified petroleum gas (LPG) stood at ₹245 per cylinder in October and is projected at ₹327 per cylinder in November.

She added that the total under-recovery for LPG in the September-end quarter stood at ₹500 crores.

Separately, Mr. Kaushal also informed analysts that Hindustan Petroleum has petrol and diesel stocks combined for twenty days. This excludes the crude that is presently being processed in their refineries.

articles.title: Stranded Iranian sailors receive urgent medical assistance in Sri Lanka
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Sri Lankan authorities facilitate transfer of 40 sailors from sanctioned oil tankers for treatment; Iranian Embassy bears expenses

Around 40 stranded Iranian sailors aboard U.S.-sanctioned oil tankers anchored just outside Sri Lanka’s territorial waters received urgent medical treatment in the island nation on Saturday (October 24, 2026), Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry said.

On Saturday (October 24, 2026), Sri Lankan authorities facilitated the transfer of the Iranian sailors from their vessels to the shore through the port of Galle in the country’s Southern Province, Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo told The Hindu . “We coordinated the transfer alone as per our humanitarian obligations. The Iranian Embassy bore all the expenses,” he said.

A senior official at the Iranian Embassy in Colombo confirmed the development and said the sailors were taken from Galle to Colombo for medical attention before leaving Sri Lanka on Saturday night (October 24, 2026), indicating they spent only a few hours on the island.

The development comes a month after The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. “pressure” through sanctions had left the Iranian vessels stranded in Sri Lankan waters. At the time, the Sri Lankan Foreign Ministry said Colombo would not be extending assistance to the sanctioned vessels, while emphasising that the secondary sanctions were part of a broader directive from Washington, D.C. and not specific to Sri Lanka. Denying media reports of U.S. pressure on Sri Lanka, Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath said the Sri Lankan government made decisions “strictly protecting the country’s sovereignty”, even as it was prepared to intervene appropriately on humanitarian grounds.

Earlier this year, Sri Lanka made headlines when a U.S. submarine attacked and sank Iranian frigate IRIS Dena in the Indian Ocean, off the island’s southern coast. At least 84 people were killed in the torpedo attack, which sent shockwaves across the region. Sri Lanka’s ruling Anura Kumara Dissanayake administration, while reiterating its commitment to a “neutral foreign policy”, directed its Navy to evacuate the injured sailors . They were subsequently treated at a public hospital in the Galle district.

articles.title: Bangladesh seeks details from Saudi Arabia on execution of two citizens: report
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The two Bangladesh nationals, a man and a woman, were executed on October 14, after being convicted of committing an “indecent act” inside a mosque in Makkah

Bangladesh has sought detailed information from Saudi Arabia about the execution of two of its citizens in the Makkah region, including the charges against them, court verdicts, manner of execution, whereabouts of their bodies and whether they had legal representation during their trials, according to a local media report.

The Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah sent a diplomatic letter to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs' branch in Makkah on October 19, seeking answers to six questions, according to a report by Bangladeshi newspaper Prothom Alo published on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
Bangladesh's Consul General in Jeddah also raised the matter with a senior Saudi foreign ministry official during a meeting the same day, the report said.
The two Bangladesh nationals, a man and a woman, were executed on October 14, after being convicted of committing an “indecent act” inside a mosque in Makkah.
The diplomatic letter seeks details of the offences, when and where they allegedly took place, the dates of arrest and certified copies of the court verdicts, the report said.

It also asks whether the death sentences were carried out by beheading or another method, where the bodies are being kept and whether they will be repatriated to Bangladesh or have already been buried in Saudi Arabia.
Bangladesh has also sought information on whether lawyers represented the two during the investigation and trial and whether they had requested legal assistance, the report said.

According to Prothom Alo , Bangladeshi officials said the country's missions did not have detailed information about the proceedings leading to the executions, including whether the two had legal representation.

A list of Bangladeshi prisoners shared by Saudi authorities in September reportedly contained allegations of adultery and an information technology-related offence involving the two, but did not specify their sentences.
Dhaka is seeking clarification on the discrepancy between those entries and the Saudi Interior Ministry's public explanation of the executions.
Bangladesh had also raised the executions with the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka, according to the Dhaka Tribune .

Bangladeshi officials said the government had not received detailed official information from Saudi authorities before learning that the executions had been carried out, the newspaper reported last week.

articles.title: Donald Trump says Audi to invest $4.2 billion in its first U.S. auto plant
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Audi confirmed the investment in a release, saying the plant would create about 4,500 jobs

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Saturday (October 24, 2026) that German automaker Audi planned to invest $4.2 billion to build its first factory in the United States, 10 days before midterm elections.
Audi confirmed the investment in a release, saying the plant would create about 4,500 jobs.

"I'm thrilled to announce a massive auto manufacturing investment in the great state of Georgia by a fantastic company," Mr. Trump said at a campaign rally ahead of the November 3 vote that will determine control of the U.S. Congress.
"Audi has just committed to invest $4.2 billion in nearby Macon, Georgia, to begin the construction next month on a massive plant that will produce 200,000 cars a year," Mr. Trump continued.
Audi, which is a unit of Volkswagen (VW), said in its release that construction was scheduled to begin next year and production in the early 2030s.

"The planned investment intends to mark a long-term commitment to the United States and to establish North America as a third major pillar of Audi's global production network alongside Europe and China," it said.
VW, long a titan of German industry, has struggled with U.S. tariffs, Chinese competition and patchy demand in Europe.

Increasing production in the United States represents an "opportunity", "provided that factories and employees in Germany also benefit from it", said Olaf Lies, president of the German region of Lower Saxony, where VW is headquartered.
In September, the 10-brand Volkswagen Group struck a deal with unions to axe up to 100,000 jobs by 2030, increasing by 50,000 the number of expected cuts across the group.
The cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry.
Mr. Trump has claimed a "roaring comeback" in American auto manufacturing in response to his aggressive trade policy.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Mr. Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products -- including autos -- and countries.

articles.title: Explosions heard in Saudi capital as airport prepares to reopen
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks
Explosions rang out in the Saudi capital on Sunday (October 25, 2026), as the kingdom was due to reopen Riyadh international airport despite repeated attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart, and has shifted the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war.
Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday (October 25, 2026) after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.
However, it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.

The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the facility was still "unsafe" and a "military target".

"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional, and local airlines — as well as staff and travellers — against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."

An AFP journalist in the city heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday (October 25, 2026), with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards Riyadh, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.

articles.title: India advises its nationals in Saudi Arabia against filming missile interceptions
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The Indian mission also shared an update about the suspension of flights from Air India and Air India Express to and from Riyadh and Dammam

India on Sunday (October 25, 2026) advised its nationals in Saudi Arabia to abide by local rules and regulations and refrain from filming or publishing information related to missile and drone interceptions.
The advisory comes amid escalating tensions in the region due to a series of drone and missile attacks targeting civilian infrastructure by Yemen’s Houthis.

"The Indian community residing in Saudi Arabia is requested to abide by local rules and regulations," the Indian Embassy said on social media while reposting the notification issued by the Directorate of Saudi Civil Defence.
"Filming, publishing, or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability," the notification said.
The Indian mission also shared an update about the suspension of flights from Air India and Air India Express to and from Riyadh and Dammam.

"Air India and Air India Express flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam will remain suspended until 7 November 2026, while services to and from Jeddah will remain suspended until 31 October 2026," it posted on social media on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
The Consulate General of India in Jeddah also shared a similar advisory.

On Saturday (October 24, 2026), the Consulate General of India in Jeddah said its 24×7 Control Rooms in Jeddah and Makkah continued to provide necessary assistance to affected Indians, with support from community associations and volunteers.
The assistance includes food, essential medicines and other immediate requirements wherever needed and feasible, it said.

The mission also said it remained in regular contact with Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Hajj and Umrah and Ministry of Foreign Affairs to address difficulties caused by the flight disruptions, particularly issues concerning visa validity and delayed departures.
Meanwhile, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is preparing to resume domestic and international flight operations on Sunday, the Gulf News web portal reported.
It also quoted the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis as saying on Sunday that air defences had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh.

articles.title: Health Wrap Episode 56 discusses early-onset Alzheimer’s, cancer research paper mills and more
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The episode discusses how Alzheimer’s disease can present in younger people, concerns about cancer research articles linked to suspected paper mills, and questions raised by families over a generic drug for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)

The 56th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu examines early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, concerns about the reliability of cancer research and challenges in accessing treatment for children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss how Alzheimer’s disease can affect younger people, the implications of unreliable cancer research, and concerns raised by families over a generic SMA drug.

The episode begins with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and how the condition can present differently in younger people. The discussion looks at changes in memory, behaviour and everyday functioning, and the challenges of recognising the disease when symptoms appear earlier in life.

Another segment examines cancer research articles flagged for suspected links to paper mills. These businesses produce and sell research papers, sometimes using fabricated data, manipulated images or other questionable research practices. The discussion looks at how unreliable publications can undermine scientific progress, affect future research and complicate efforts to assess the evidence behind medical findings. It also highlights the need for careful investigation, as an article being flagged for suspected links to a paper mill does not, by itself, establish research misconduct.

The episode also looks at concerns raised by families of children living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Keralam over a generic drug used to treat the rare genetic condition. The concerns have brought questions about the safety, quality and effectiveness of medicines into focus. The discussion examines the importance of reliable information about treatment, regulatory oversight and the challenges families face in accessing medicines for rare diseases, where treatment costs can be a significant barrier.

The final segment revisits the history of Alzheimer’s disease through the case of Auguste Deter. In 1901, German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer began documenting the symptoms of Deter, a 51-year-old woman who experienced changes in memory, behaviour and her ability to carry out everyday activities. Her symptoms differed from cases he had typically encountered. After her death in 1906, Alzheimer examined her brain and identified changes that contributed to the understanding of the condition later named after him. The segment explores Deter’s experience and the role of clinical observation and patient documentation in the history of medical research.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

articles.title: KSSP supports distribution of generic drugs for SMA patients in Keralam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.
In a statement, KSSP president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients.
The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.

The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. They claimed that the department’s decision is not merely aimed at saving public funds. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.

articles.title: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions

Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding , following the devastating floods in August.

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022 , and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.
The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

articles.title: Starshield | The non-state sovereigns
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Elon Musk limited Ukraine’s access to the military-grade network of Starlink after Trum pcriticised Kyiv’s strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure

On October 14, Ukrainian soldiers using drones to attack Russian forces in Zaporizhzhia and elsewhere started to find many of their machines were losing satellite connectivity. Given Ukraine’s extensive and largely successful use of drones in the war, the anomaly was noticeable, forcing operators to abandon missions.

Experts later traced the problem to a satellite communications service provided by U.S.-based SpaceX, called Starshield. A week later, The Wall Street Journal reported the disruption had been deliberate: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had personally asked for the connectivity to be throttled. Where the order first originated has been disputed, in Mr. Musk’s office or in the White House. But wherever it did, the fact remains: Mr. Musk was able to take para-state action in a war between two sovereign countries. (On October 22, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had asked Mr. Musk to restore connectivity.)

SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites in low-earth orbit that provide Internet connectivity to users on the ground. Starshield uses the same constellation to provide secure communications important to national security, with stronger data encryption; its other services, including remote-sensing, use specialised satellites. Ukraine uses Starshield because Russia’s invasion in early 2022 has damaged the eastern European nation’s telecom infrastructure.

By December 2024, the Pentagon had also arranged for Ukraine to access Starshield through roughly 3,000 terminals. Today, its forces use the service to track enemy positions and supply routes and to intercept drones, with the Starlink satellites relaying information.

Mr. Trump has been insisting Ukraine stop attacking Russia’s oil refineries over his worries about surging international oil prices, primed by his war in West Asia. When Mr. Trump objected once more on October 10, Mr. Musk chipped in that Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had gone too far. Four days later, Ukrainian soldiers felt the pinch.

For decades now, private contractors have supplied armies with arms, intelligence, and logistical support. However, the armies had physical ownership of and control over many of the weapons they purchased. With Starshield, however, the provider continued to retain the ability to change the operating conditions of the ‘assistance’ even after the customer had begun using it — like a grenade launcher that could launch grenades to 150 m on most days but suddenly launched only to five metres on one, because you were not fighting your war the way the manufacturer preferred.

The existence of such an entity is the basis of Mr. Musk’s parastate power. Ordinarily, the decision to stop or withhold a country’s military operations would involve political leaders and defence officials. Now, however, Starshield has well and truly complicated the relationship between public authority and private ownership. Perhaps it was a matter of time.

In 2022, Mr. Musk refused Ukraine’s request to activate Starlink connectivity near Sevastopol, the largest city in Crimea, which Russia has annexed, to enable Ukrainian forces to target Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. Mr. Musk later expressed some consternation about the conflict escalating — a compunction he seems to have lost since, even as his own relationship with Mr. Trump has soared and plummeted. Nonetheless, the fact that the concerns of a single non-state actor could matter at all — an absurd notion in an earlier era — has become a strategic reality. Subsequent Pentagon contracts have sought, at least in part, to formalise the relationship between Starlink and the U.S. military.

Today’s armies, and their wars, increasingly depend on satellite communications, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence, all of which private contractors can develop and package at speed and deploy at scale. Musk’s actions with Starshield last week have revealed that military action had until recently depended, perhaps passively, on the lack of such speed and scale as one kind of safeguard. Now that their importance is shrinking, armies of the present and future must deliberate on what can replace them.
