articles.title: Feral dogs ‘a major threat’ to vultures in Thar desert, study finds
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Vultures spend half as long on carcasses at an open dump site than at dog-free enclosures, the scientists observed

In the heart of Rajasthan’s Thar desert , on the outskirts of the agro-pastoralist landscape of Bikaner, is a dumpsite of livestock carcasses where, traditionally, a feeding frenzy plays out among multiple species of beasts and birds everyday.

Importantly, every winter, a large number of migratory Himalayan and Eurasian griffon, whose numbers have dwindled catastrophically in the country, congregate at this dumpsite, located in the northwestern corner of Jorbeer Conservation Reserve of Bikaner. Other scavengers here are Egyptian vultures, steppe eagles, black ibises, cattle egrets and wild pigs, which feast on dead cattle, horses, camels, sheep and goats.

Now, a new study published in the journal Biological Conservation has found that perennially free-ranging dogs pose a serious threat to vultures here. This finding comes in the backdrop of other studies that have tracked the catastrophic decline in vulture populations in India : the raptor numbers plummeted by over 90% in the 1990s, largely due to the veterinary use of the anti-inflammatory drug diclofenac in livestock. When the cattle died, their poisonous carcasses killed the birds that fed on them in large numbers.
In several parts of India, vultures went extinct. An older study even corelated vulture decline to increased human deaths from a burgeoning feral dog population and the spread of rabies.

“As vulture recovery efforts continue, the presence of dogs at supplementary feeding sites [dumpsites] may hinder vulture access through direct competition and aggressive interference,” cautions the new paper.

India’s vulture populations have historically been sustained by livestock carcass dumpsites, but with dogs increasingly in the mix, the scientists found that vultures spent about half as long on carcasses at the open Bikaner dumpsite than at dog-free enclosures. “Dog presence also altered their temporal feeding patterns, restricting vulture activity largely to the afternoon, whereas in the absence of dogs, feeding was distributed more evenly across daylight hours,” the paper added.

As dogs can consume large amounts of meat, it reduces food availability for vultures too; the canines also chase away the birds, reducing their access to carcasses. The paper concludes that dogs are “a major threat to vultures” here.

Dumpsites or ‘supplementary feeding sites’ are places where carcasses are regularly accessible to scavengers at a fixed location. In Europe and Africa they are usually managed “vulture restaurants” offering safe, drug-free carrion, co-author of the paper, Abi T. Vanak of Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment, told The Hindu .

“In India, traditional livestock carcass dumps were never designed for vultures, but their large and predictable carcass supply made them function as de facto feeding sites for vultures, as at Jorbeer in Bikaner,” he added.

While dumpsites function as a “highly predictable food resource[s]” for vultures, it is imperative that they are managed adequately, said the paper conceding that the “predictability” of such feeding sites “may promote the habituation of vultures,” diminishing their natural foraging activity across the reserve. Moreover, competitively superior species, such as large griffons, are more likely to monopolise the majority of this food resource available, thereby displacing subordinate species.

The impact of dogs on wildlife has been well documented.: the canines are known to have contributed to the extinction of 11 vertebrate species around the world. In India, they are known to prey on over 80 species, including black bucks, desert foxes and olive ridley turtles, according to a paper in the journal Animal Conservation . They have even been documented attacking snow leopards in Ladakh.

Prof. Vanak said that setting up more dispersed dog-proof feeding sites could encourage broader landscape level foraging by vultures, thus reducing their dependence on a single site. “Our study shows that conserving vulture populations will require more strategic management of food sources, including managing the populations of dogs, and creating vulture ‘safe zones’ where they can feed in peace,” he added.

articles.title: Another worker succumbs to injuries in Vellore; cracker unit owner arrested
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Collector P.S. Leela Alex handed over ₹4 lakh ex-gratia from Chief Minister’s Public Relief Fund to family members of the deceased workers
A 35-year-old firecracker manufacturing unit owner was arrested by Anaicut police in Vellore after an explosion in the unit killed two workers.

The arrested person was identified as Hari Prasad, who runs a cracker unit in Chinna Anaicut village, that comes under Anaicut Panchayat Union in the district. He was nabbed by a special team from his hideout in Jawadhu Hills. A case was registered and he was lodged at Central Prison in Vellore.

On Wednesday, R. Gayathri, 41, a worker, was killed on the spot after an explosion occured in the firecracker unit. Another worker U. Sangeetha, 45, sustained 96 per cent burns in the incident. Both workers belong to Kottaiyur village near the unit.
The workers were packing firecrackers in the unit when the explosion occurred. The building was razed to the ground.

The injured worker, Sangeetha was admitted at Government Medical College Hospital in Vellore where she succumbed to burn injuries on Friday. Collector P.S. Leela Alex handed over ₹4 lakh ex-gratia from Chief Minister’s Public Relief Fund to family members of the deceased workers. Based on orders of Ms. Alex, license of the firecracker manufacturing unit was cancelled, and the unit was sealed by revenue officials.

articles.title: Andhra CM alerts officials about the cyclone in Bay of Bengal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: He called for completion of 36 priority irrigation as per schedule

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu directed the officials to be alert and take precautionary measures in view of the likelihood of heavy rainfall under the influence of the cyclone developing in the Bay of Bengal.
He instructed them to make effective use of rainfall in the coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema districts by filling reservoirs and irrigation tanks.

In a review meeting with officials of the Water Resources Department (WRD) at his camp office Friday (October 23, 2026) evening, Mr. Chandrababu Naidu called for implementing a comprehensive action plan covering flood management, water management and disaster management.

బంగాళాఖాతంలో వాయుగుండం ఏర్పడడంతో పాటు తుపాను ముప్పు పొంచి ఉన్న నేపథ్యంలో గౌరవ ముఖ్యమంత్రి శ్రీ నారా చంద్రబాబు నాయుడు అధికారులతో సమీక్షించారు. రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వ ప్రధాన కార్యదర్శి శ్రీ సాయి ప్రసాద్, ఆర్టీజీఎస్ అధికారులు ఈ సమీక్ష లో పాల్గొన్నారు. ప్రజలకు ముందస్తు సూచనలు జారీ చేయడంతో పాటు, అధికార యంత్రాంగం అప్రమత్తంగా ఉండాలని సీఎం ఆదేశించారు. తూర్పుమధ్య బంగాళాఖాతంలో కేంద్రీకృతమైన అల్పపీడనం తుపానుగా బలపడే అవకాశం ఉందని, మంగళ, బుధవారాల్లో కోస్తాంధ్రలో భారీ నుంచి అతిభారీ వర్షాలు కురిసే అవకాశముందని అధికారులు సీఎంకు వివరించారు. ఈ నేపథ్యంలో తీరప్రాంతాల్లో బలమైన ఈదురుగాలులు వీచే అవకాశం ఉన్నందున మత్స్యకారులు సముద్రంలోకి వెళ్లకుండా చర్యలు తీసుకోవాలని సీఎం సూచించారు. తుఫాన్ ప్రభావిత ప్రాంతాల్లోని లోతట్టు కాలనీల ప్రజలను అప్రమత్తం చేయాలని, అత్యవసర సహాయం, సమాచారం కోసం టోల్ ఫ్రీ నంబర్లను సంప్రదించేలా అందుబాటులోకి తేవాలని సీఎం ఆదేశించారు. #AndhraPradesh

He told the officials to ensure maximum benefits for farmers by preventing the wastage of rainwater, conserving available water and managing irrigation resources efficiently, and ordered that the Chintalapudi lift irrigation project work be resumed next month.

The CM instructed the WRD to complete the construction of 36 identified priority projects in accordance with the prescribed targets and prepare an action plan to make all the projects operational by December 2028. He stated that the government’s objective was to provide tap water to every household and irrigation water to every acre.
He stressed the need to strengthen the existing canal network and enhance water storage capacity, and suggested that plans be made to install solar panels along canals to generate electricity.

Further, Mr. Chandrababu Naidu made it clear that there should be no compromise on technical standards in the construction of the Polavaram project and called for completion of Polavaram right and left main canals by March 2027.
Officials informed the CM that 90.20% of the Polavaram project’s civil works had been completed and work on Gap-1 and Gap-2 of the main earth-cum-rockfill dam was progressing at a brisk pace.

He told the officials to initiate an action plan to link the Godavari and Penna rivers, and transfer Godavari water to the Cauvery. He also asked them to examine the feasibility of constructing barrages at Vaikuntapuram and Chodavaram, upstream and downstream of Prakasam Barrage, to store 14 TMC ft of water.
He also proposed the development of a navigation system for inland water transport from Bhadrachalam to Visakhapatnam via Rajamahendravaram and Vijayawada.

articles.title: Govt. to fund half the cost of deepwater wells, recover money from winners
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: That recovery clause, set out in newly issued operational guidelines, is the scheme's central bargain — the government carries early geological risk and keeps a claim on any upside

The government will pay up to half the cost of risky deepwater exploration wells under its ₹84,084 crore Samudra Manthan scheme, but expects to be repaid from revenue if a well finds oil or gas. If it finds nothing, the State absorbs the loss.
That recovery clause, set out in newly issued operational guidelines, is the scheme's central bargain — the government carries early geological risk and keeps a claim on any upside.

The guidelines say recovery starts after seven years of commercial production, or once the operator has recouped 50% of its exploration and development costs, whichever comes first. Repayment comes in annual instalments, with no inflation indexation.

The scheme will support 60 wells in deepwater (deeper than 400 metres) and ultra-deepwater (deeper than 1,500 metres) areas. Of these, 56 exploratory wells get up to 50% of actual cost, capped at ₹675 crore per well, the guidelines said, adding that four stratigraphic wells, drilled to study rock layers, get up to 100%, capped at ₹1,350 crore each. Only state-run firms or consortia they lead can apply.
Payment is milestone-based — 40% when drilling reaches 40% of the approved depth and 60% on completion and approval of the well report.
By these caps, well support alone could reach ₹43,200 crore, about half the total outlay. The guidelines did not give a component-wise budget split.
The guidelines also lay out a strict eligibility test. Only blocks or areas awarded under the Revenue Sharing Contract regime qualify.
These are the blocks awarded in bid rounds since 2016. Production-sharing and coal-bed methane blocks, awarded prior to that, are excluded unless the government notifies otherwise.

Importantly, only exploration wells or wells drilled to find new resources qualify for the grant. Development wells, which are drilled to bring an already discovered resource into production, are not covered. Sidetrack well costs are also not covered.

The scheme aims to cut India's heavy reliance on imported hydrocarbons. The guidelines say it will run through FY2030-31, with FY2026-27 as a preparatory year and spending in FY 2027-28 to FY2030-31 as Phase I.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the scheme in his August 15, 2025 Independence Day speech, saying India wants "to work in a mission mode towards finding oil and gas reserves under the sea".

Govt. to fund half the cost of deepwater wells, recover money from winners

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes

That recovery clause, set out in newly issued operational guidelines, is the scheme's central bargain — the government carries early geological risk and keeps a claim on any upside

The government will pay up to half the cost of risky deepwater exploration wells under its ₹84,084 crore Samudra Manthan scheme, but expects to be repaid from revenue if a well finds oil or gas. If it finds nothing, the State absorbs the loss.

That recovery clause, set out in newly issued operational guidelines, is the scheme's central bargain — the government carries early geological risk and keeps a claim on any upside.

The guidelines say recovery starts after seven years of commercial production, or once the operator has recouped 50% of its exploration and development costs, whichever comes first. Repayment comes in annual instalments, with no inflation indexation.

The scheme will support 60 wells in deepwater (deeper than 400 metres) and ultra-deepwater (deeper than 1,500 metres) areas. Of these, 56 exploratory wells get up to 50% of actual cost, capped at ₹675 crore per well, the guidelines said, adding that four stratigraphic wells, drilled to study rock layers, get up to 100%, capped at ₹1,350 crore each. Only state-run firms or consortia they lead can apply.

Payment is milestone-based — 40% when drilling reaches 40% of the approved depth and 60% on completion and approval of the well report.

By these caps, well support alone could reach ₹43,200 crore, about half the total outlay. The guidelines did not give a component-wise budget split.

The guidelines also lay out a strict eligibility test. Only blocks or areas awarded under the Revenue Sharing Contract regime qualify.

These are the blocks awarded in bid rounds since 2016. Production-sharing and coal-bed methane blocks, awarded prior to that, are excluded unless the government notifies otherwise.

Importantly, only exploration wells or wells drilled to find new resources qualify for the grant. Development wells, which are drilled to bring an already discovered resource into production, are not covered. Sidetrack well costs are also not covered.

Petroleum Secretary Neeraj Mittal, in the preface to the guidelines, called the scheme "the most ambitious upstream oil and gas intervention undertaken in recent times" and said it could add "more than 600 million tonnes of oil equivalent" to India's reserves.

Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday (October 25, 2026) after a two-week closure following strikes from Yemen's Houthis on the Saudi capital, though the Iran-backed group warned of more to come.

The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on Riyadh's airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target".

articles.title: What is the importance of the UN Loss and Damage Fund’s payout to Nepal? | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions

Story so far: The United Nations’ climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has approved a $21.6 million pay out (approx. ₹205 crore) to the Nepal government to help with rebuilding , following the devastating floods in August.

Formally, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), was set up to help developing countries that are particularly vulnerable to climate change respond to economic and non-economic losses, including from extreme weather and slow-onset events. It operates under the financial mechanism of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Governments agreed to create it at COP27 in 2022 , and its Governing Instrument was adopted at COP28 in 2023.

As of March 15, 2026, 27 countries had pledged $822.06 million (approx. ₹7,809.6 crore), with $629.70 million (₹5,982 crore) in grant contributions. Its start-up allocation is $342 million with at least half of it reserved for small island developing States and least developed countries. Its first call for funding requests drew 176 requests from 119 countries worth about $2.8 billion (₹26,600 crore). In July the Board deferred decisions on those requests to December.

It is the first time the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country. The Board took the decision at its first “extraordinary meeting,” held virtually on October 22, 2026. It also agreed to pilot, during the start-up phase, an approach allowing Nepal to submit a request outside the closed submission window. Any further such submissions will need separate Board decisions, and the Secretariat will assess lessons for the Fund’s long-term model.

On August 26, 2026, an ice-and-rock avalanche, that experts say is linked to climate changed from human-accelerated global warming, set off flooding along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli–Narayani river system. Nepal estimates economic losses of at least $2.69 billion and recovery needs of at least $4.71 billion. The decision comes weeks before COP31 opens in Turkiye.

The $21.6 million approved by the Board includes $1.6 million in oversight fees, which are paid to the organisations that implement projects to cover the cost of supervising how money is used. Nepal has been invited to submit a funding request, which the Board will consider at its tenth meeting in Manila in December. Money would be released only after that approval.
The Fund has not publicly said how much cash it holds beyond signed contributions, and disbursement depends on donors honouring pledges.

Since its creation at COP27, the Fund has had to show that pledges translate into money for affected countries. The United States, the largest historical emitter, had pledged $17.5 million under President Joe Biden. In January 2025, the Trump administration withdrew the US representatives from the Fund’s board which was part of the US’ larger exit out of the Paris Agreement. At the time, pledges stood at about $741 million.

Jawad Khalid, a climate finance specialist writing for the Lowy Institute, an independent Australian think tank, argued that the Fund “still operates like a conventional development fund” rather than an emergency mechanism. “Its single funding cycle runs eleven steps, from origination through technical review to board approval. The Fund is hosted by the World Bank, which serves as its interim trustee,” he wrote in a piece.

Ajay Mathur, a former Director General of the International Solar Alliance, called the step “landmark” in a media statement. He cautioned that the sum is less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction cost. He noted that cash would flow only after further project proposals are cleared, risking delays to relief.

Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, said in a media statement that while the Fund “took a historic first step” it it “cannot be a one-off.” He said no country should have to wait seven weeks, through “historic letters and relentless pressure,” to unlock an emergency meeting, and called for a permanent rapid-response system that moves support “in days, not months.” He said developed countries insisted the decision must not set a precedent or prejudge the long-term model, adding: “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions.”

Others read the decision more positively. Raju Pandit Chhetri, the Least Developed Countries’ lead climate finance negotiator, said it showed countries could reach “swift, effective consensus” and set “a strong precedent.”

articles.title: What happens inside the brain during a stroke?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The first few hours of a stroke determine how damaged the brain can become. Knowing the signs and seeking timely medical help is crucial

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.

Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.

An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.

The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.

There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.

In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.

Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.

The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.
It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.

🚀 Science, Tech & Environment 📅 25 Oct 2026 • IN-APP NEWSPAPER PRINT EDITION

What happens inside the brain during a stroke?

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports

The first few hours of a stroke determine how damaged the brain can become. Knowing the signs and seeking timely medical help is crucial

A stroke is an urgent situation where either the flow of blood to the brain is cut off, or there is a rupture of the blood vessels in the brain. Oxygen and glucose are the two elements essential for brain activity. Interruption of their supply results in impairment of brain activity and eventual damage of brain tissues -- and this damage occurs in minutes. The first few hours of a stroke, therefore, determine how damaged the brain can become.

Strokes can be categorised into ischemic strokes and haemorrhagic strokes. In ischemic strokes, the stroke occurs due to the blocking of an artery by a blood clot. In haemorrhagic strokes, there is a rupture of the blood vessel, which leads to blood in the brain tissue. Regardless of the type of stroke, the result is damage to the brain tissue, which can result in vital body functions including speaking, movement, vision, memory and coordination becoming impaired.

An ischemic stroke is accompanied by oxygen starvation of the affected brain tissue. Due to insufficient energy resources, brain cells cannot function normally. The chemical composition of the brain cells, therefore, changes, which results in the accumulation of toxic substances that harm brain cells and other structures. With continued oxygen starvation, cells continue to deteriorate. The damage, however, does not occur uniformly. In the central area of the brain (core) where oxygen starvation is critical, damage can occur rapidly and irreversibly. Around this area, there is a zone called the ischemic penumbra. Here, even if blood flow is low, brain cells can survive for a certain period of time. They can be saved if blood flow is restored promptly.

The effect of bleeding in a haemorrhagic stroke is brought about by the leaking of blood into the brain when there is a rupture of a blood vessel. This may lead to injury of brain cells, and also interfere with proper blood and cerebral spinal fluid flow in the brain.

There are only so many minutes that the brain can withstand interrupted blood flow. Brain cells (neurons) begins to undergo irreversible damage within 3 to 5 minutes of interrupted blood flow. With each minute that goes by, 1.9 million neurons, i.e. 32 neurons per second, die due to lack of oxygenation, which is why we emphasise that ‘time is brain’. The first few hours are critical since at this point, one needs to assess what kind of stroke it is and start appropriate treatment.

In some cases of ischemic stroke, intravenous thrombolysis, the administration of drugs that dissolve the clot within the blood vessels, might be given in the first 4.5 hours after symptoms develop. In some patients with large vessel blockage, there might be indications for mechanical thrombectomy. In simple terms, a mechanical thrombectomy involves the removal of the clot using special equipment, and it might be done up to 24 hours after the patient was last seen without symptoms. In cases of haemorrhagic strokes, others strategies must be employed: this includes blood pressure control, correction of the consequences of taking blood thinners, management of intracranial pressure, and surgical procedures, where necessary.

Not all patients automatically qualify for all interventions. There are other issues that have to be taken into account, including the patient’s medical status, imaging studies, timing of stroke symptoms, and dangers involved in the therapy. Even some of those who come after these time windows, can still be eligible for certain treatment procedures after imaging is done.

The effects of a stroke vary, depending on the site and degree of damage within the brain. Movement centres can be damaged leading to weakness or paralysis that usually affects one side of the body. Speech centres could be damaged causing speech problems and comprehension difficulties or trouble reading and writing. A stroke involving the visual pathways leads to a sudden loss of vision or partial visual fields. If the cerebellum or the brainstem is involved, there could be a problem with dizziness, poor coordination, problems swallowing, double vision or loss of balance. There could also be memory, attention and decision-making problems and problems with emotional regulation.

It is important to know and understand these symptoms since sometimes a stroke occurs without the characteristic facial drooping or arm weakness of the disease.

Medical teams will continue monitoring the condition of the patient, controlling blood pressure and preventing additional harm to him or her. In case the condition of the patient becomes satisfactory, it is likely that he or she will be offered physiotherapy, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy and cognitive therapy.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: In the 56th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu, Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss health issues that highlight the importance of early diagnosis, reliable scientific evidence and access to treatment. The episode looks at how early-onset Alzheimer’s disease can present differently in people below the age of 65, with symptoms affecting language, vision and other thinking abilities, sometimes making diagnosis more challenging. It also examines concerns over more than 4,000 cancer research papers flagged for suspected links to paper mills, businesses that produce and sell research papers, sometimes using fabricated data or manipulated findings. The discussion explains why such concerns matter for the reliability of scientific evidence, while noting that flagged papers require further investigation. The episode also looks at concerns raised by families of children living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Keralam over a generic drug. With SMA affecting the nerve cells that control muscle movement, treatment and ongoing care can be crucial. Families need clear information about the safety, effectiveness and quality of medicines, alongside affordable and accessible treatment options for this rare genetic condition.

articles.title: Panel formed to probe spurious liquor death claims in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas; report in 15 days
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Some villagers have claimed that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Dewas district between September 27 and October 16

The Madhya Pradesh Government has constituted a five-member committee to investigate claims that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district , officials said on Sunday (October 25, 2026).
The panel will submit its report within 15 days, they said.
Ujjain divisional Commissioner constituted the committee after conflicting claims over the deaths.
Some villagers have claimed that at least 10 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Dewas district between September 27 and October 16.

The district administration had earlier dismissed the claims as false and misleading. It later said viscera samples of two deceased persons have been sent to a forensic science laboratory (FSL) for examination. The cause of death would become clear after the reports are received, it added.

The administration said 10 persons died in Chandana village between October 1 and 15, but denied that any of the deaths was caused by spurious liquor. It attributed the deaths to old age, common illnesses, brain haemorrhage and "deterioration of health due to excessive alcohol consumption".

Ujjain Additional District Magistrate Pratham Kaushik will head the probe committee, which includes Mandsaur Additional Superintendent of Police Ramsanehi Mishra, Ratlam Sub-Divisional Police Officer Lekhraj Meena, Ujjain divisional flying squad Deputy Excise Commissioner Harshvardhan Rai and Regional Director of Public Health and Medical Education Dr Deepak Kumar Pippal.

The panel will conduct a detailed and impartial inquiry into the causes and circumstances of the deaths, along with the related technical and administrative aspects, and submit a factual report within 15 days, according to the Ujjain divisional Commissioner's order.

Madhya Pradesh Congress president Jitu Patwari has claimed that 22 persons died after consuming spurious liquor in Chandana, Binjana and adjoining areas over the past month, while at least 40 people suffered damage to their eyesight.
The Opposition party leader has accused the administration of concealing the deaths and shielding the "liquor mafia".

articles.title: New form of carbon found: diamondiyne
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The Hindu’s weekly Science for All newsletter explains all things Science, without the jargon
Scientists have created a new form of carbon called diamondiyne. It is a three-dimensional network of carbon atoms that resembles a diamond but with a more open structure.
Researchers first proposed the existence of this form more than three decades ago and it has finally been synthesised. The findings were reported in the journal Angewandte Chemie .

Carbon atoms can bond together to form crystals of different shapes, called allotropes. The three most famous ones are graphite, diamond, and graphene. While in diamond each carbon atom bonds to four neighbours, in the graphene the atoms form a flat sheet. Diamondiyne is more akin to diamond but it more closely resembles two open jungle gyms — the grid of cages you see in parks where children can climb and swing from — pushed through each other, with more spacious cages, with more room within the structure than diamonds.

Scientists took so long to create this allotrope because one of its chemical building blocks is unstable and because if the bonds do not connect properly in the process of making it, they can be difficult to undo.

The researchers who succeeded, from the University of Gothenburg, Stock University, and the Chalmers University of Technology, all in Sweden, did so by making the material at a boundary between water and chloroform, with the chemical reaction slowly releasing the building blocks and allowing them to link up at a rate the team could control. (The ‘y’ in the material’s name comes from the presence of carbon-carbon triple bonds.)

The process — which could take around a week — produced thin films of carbon covering around five square centimetres each. The researchers could control their thickness by slowing down or speeding up the reaction, from a few nanometres to up to 60 nanometres.
The team used spectroscopy and electron microscopy to confirm the films contained small diamondiyne crystals. However, it was present only to the tune of 1% of the reaction yield.
Scientists often pursue research like this in order to discover what forms matter can take and how the ways in which their atoms are arranged control their properties as a material.

Carbon in particular poses an interesting case because while diamond is extremely hard and an electrical insulator, graphite is soft and conducts electricity, yet both are allotropes of the same element. By extension, synthesising the new allotrope has reinforced the notion that scientists can potentially create materials with radically different properties but without changing their chemical composition.
And some discoveries could eventually lead to a material that might be useful in electronics, storing energy or some other technology that the world is looking for.

The cage-like structure of diamondiyne also offers the additional prospect of containing other atoms within. Synthesising diamondiyne confirms to scientists that the prediction more than 30 years ago was correct, which in turn validates the process scientists used to make that prediction.

articles.title: FPIs withdraw ₹48,056 cr from equities in October so far amid elevated crude oil prices
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes

articles.title: Raj Thackeray deletes PM Modi-Adani documentary from social media after Mumbai Police chief's request
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Meanwhile, MNS leaders were also surprised by the removal of the documentary, considering it was screened in one of the party's shakhas on Saturday

Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday (October 25, 2026) said he has deleted a documentary on Prime Minister Narendra Modi and industrialist Gautam Adani from his social media handles following a request from the Mumbai Police Commissioner.
Mr. Thackeray claimed that the film, made by Hotmail founder Sabir Bhatia, had already garnered over 48 lakh views on X after being posted to enlighten the public.
The MNS chief said he has been raising the issue of close ties between Mr. Adani and PM Modi since January 2026, before the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation elections.

"The Mumbai and Maharashtra Police are the most efficient police force in the country, and I have always had respect for them in my heart. I am just honouring the request made by the head of such a Mumbai Police," he said in a post on X.
He said the documentary provides complete information on how old the friendship between Mr. Adani and PM Modi is.

Mr. Thackeray noted that while Sabir Bhatia produced the documentary recently, he had already delivered a major presentation back in January 2026 at his residence Shivteerth, illustrating how the Adani Group is effectively setting out to swallow the entire nation.
That presentation received an exceptional response, and those videos remain available on his social media to this day, and some clips were incorporated into the documentary, he said.
Meanwhile, MNS leaders were also surprised by the removal of the documentary, considering it was screened in one of the party's shakhas on Saturday (October 24).

articles.title: ACB seizes ₹2.4 lakh unaccounted cash from HMWSSB Joint Director
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: According to the ACB, it received an anonymous call alleging that a senior HMWSSB official had collected cash illegally and was carrying it while returning home from office

The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) seized ₹2.4 lakh in unaccounted cash from the possession of Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) Joint Director A. Srinivas during a vehicle check on Raj Bhavan Road on Friday (October 24, 2026) night.

According to the ACB, it received an anonymous call alleging that a senior HMWSSB official had collected cash illegally and was carrying it while returning home from office. Based on the information, the ACB City Range-II team kept surveillance on the official.

At around 7 p.m. on October 24, officials intercepted a Maruti Swift car opposite Metro Residency Apartments on Raj Bhavan Road. The vehicle was found to belong to Mr. Srinivas, who was travelling in it. During the search, ACB officials found ₹2.4 lakh in unaccounted cash in his possession.
The ACB said Mr. Srinivas failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for possessing the cash while returning from office and gave inconsistent versions when questioned.
The cash was seized under a panchanama for verification of the alleged corruption angle. The ACB said further necessary action would be taken and the Income Tax Department would be informed.

articles.title: Congress cites former Supreme Court judge’s memoir; questions independence of judiciary under Modi government
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Jairam Ramesh shared a media report which quoted the pre-publication manuscript of Justice Kaul’s memoir ‘Without Fear of Favour’ as stating that former Chief Justice of India Justice D.Y. Chandrachud was “too deferential to the Government” when it came to appointments

Citing former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul's yet-to-be-released memoir, the Congress on Sunday (October 25, 2026) flagged "serious questions" regarding the independence of the judiciary under the Modi government and asserted that the institution tasked with upholding the Constitution must remain free from the pressures of those in power.

Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report which quoted the pre-publication manuscript of Justice Kaul's memoir 'Without Fear of Favour' as stating that former Chief Justice of India Justice D.Y. Chandrachud was "too deferential to the Government" when it came to appointments.

In his post in Hindi on X, Mr. Ramesh said, "A book by former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul has raised serious questions regarding the independence of the judiciary during the tenure of the Modi government."

Justice Kaul highlights several concerning incidents — government interference in the appointment of judges, attempts to secure government approval prior to Collegium meetings, and the government's absurd questioning regarding the caste of a judge belonging to a minority community, Mr. Ramesh said.
Matters that many were previously hesitant to discuss openly have now been documented by Justice Kaul with measured, deliberate language, Mr. Ramesh said.

"Strikingly, a former Chief Justice of India (CJI) has not denied that discussions with the government take place prior to judicial appointments. When former CJI Justice Chandrachud acknowledges that the government engages with the CJI and plays a role in the appointment process, the concerns surrounding judicial independence become even more profound," Mr. Ramesh said.

Equally grave is Justice Kaul's revelation that, after a Bench he presided over raised the possibility of reconsidering certain aspects of a court ruling in a PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) case, the matter was reassigned to a different bench without any consultation with him, he said.
"This points to the extent of the government's day-to-day interference in the functioning of the Supreme Court," Mr. Ramesh said.

"When there is pressure to obtain government approval for judicial appointments, and when benches hearing sensitive cases are altered, one must ask — in the interest of safeguarding democracy — if this does not constitute pressure on the judiciary and an erosion of its independence, then what does?" the Congress leader said.

"The institution tasked with upholding the Constitution must remain free from the pressures of those in power. In a democracy, the independence of the judiciary is not merely an option; it is an absolute necessity," Mr. Ramesh asserted.

articles.title: Stalin calls on DMK cadres to prepare to oust TVK-led government soon in Tamil Nadu
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Even those who had voted for the TVK had been regretting their decision, said the DMK president while speaking in Chennai

DMK president M.K. Stalin on Sunday (October 25, 2026) wondered whether the TVK-led government in Tamil Nadu, headed by Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, would last even six months and urged his party workers to be prepared to oust the government.

Speaking at a marriage function in Chennai, Mr. Stalin said when the DMK-led alliance won the 2021 Assembly election and he took charge as Chief Minister, he had told reporters that his government would deliver good governance that even those who had not voted for the alliance would regret not having voted for it. However, he said today, those who had voted for the TVK had been regretting their decision.

“Under this government, newspapers carry reports every day of rising prices of essential commodities, administrative failures, sexual offences, murders and robberies. On one side, there are power cuts, while on the other, reports have been appearing for the past five or six days about children being kidnapped,” he said.

He said the government had formed a special force called the Singappen Special Force . “Now, a situation has arisen in which another force has to be formed to protect the Singappen Special Force,” he said.

Referring to Mr. Vijay’s rhetoric during the 2026 election campaign that the electoral battle was between only two parties — the TVK and the DMK — Mr. Stalin said after the TVK-led government came to power, the contest had become one between power cuts and murders. “But now, the situation has changed to a fight between sexual violence and the proliferation of narcotic drugs. Now, the people of Tamil Nadu must have clearly understood who the real evil force is,” Mr. Stalin said.

“I had said this government would last only for six months. Now, the situation has reached a point whether this government would even last for six months,” Mr. Stalin said, urging DMK cadres to prepare to oust the government.
Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam / Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam / Tamil Nadu / MK Stalin

articles.title: Serbia enters into elections amid ascending students’ movement against SNS
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: A leaderless student movement in Serbia now poses the biggest threat to right-wing SNS; high voter turnout expected

Serbia votes on Sunday (October 25, 2026) in what is set to be its most fiercely contested parliamentary election in more than 14 years, as a student-led movement seeks to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic.

The snap vote is the culmination of nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people, a tragedy widely blamed on corruption.
The disaster triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

The Students' List, a selection of candidates backed by the largely leaderless movement, now poses the biggest challenge to Mr. Vucic's right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has dominated politics throughout its tenure.
Eighteen electoral lists are vying for seats in Serbia's 250-member Parliament, but polls suggest the contest is largely a choice between the ruling party and the student-backed list.
Several leading opposition parties have opted not to run, instead urging supporters to back the students.
An unusually high turnout is expected among Serbia's 6.4 million registered voters.
In the decades since Milosevic fell, when around 70% cast ballots to oust him, parliamentary turnout has declined, averaging just over 55% during SNS rule.
For nearly two years, students have staged rallies and marched across the Balkan nation to reach voters directly and counter the SNS's media machine.

Their protests have regularly drawn huge crowds, with a final pre-election rally in Belgrade on Thursday (October 22, 2026) drawing around 1,50,000 people to the streets, according to an independent protest monitor.
Serbia's protesting students rally to mark 7 months since train station tragedy
Thousands rally in Belgrade against crackdown on student-led protests

articles.title: Health Wrap Episode 56 discusses early-onset Alzheimer’s, cancer research paper mills and more
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The episode discusses how Alzheimer’s disease can present in younger people, concerns about cancer research articles linked to suspected paper mills, and questions raised by families over a generic drug for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)

The 56th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu examines early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, concerns about the reliability of cancer research and challenges in accessing treatment for children with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA).

Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss how Alzheimer’s disease can affect younger people, the implications of unreliable cancer research, and concerns raised by families over a generic SMA drug.

The episode begins with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease and how the condition can present differently in younger people. The discussion looks at changes in memory, behaviour and everyday functioning, and the challenges of recognising the disease when symptoms appear earlier in life.

Another segment examines cancer research articles flagged for suspected links to paper mills. These businesses produce and sell research papers, sometimes using fabricated data, manipulated images or other questionable research practices. The discussion looks at how unreliable publications can undermine scientific progress, affect future research and complicate efforts to assess the evidence behind medical findings. It also highlights the need for careful investigation, as an article being flagged for suspected links to a paper mill does not, by itself, establish research misconduct.

The episode also looks at concerns raised by families of children living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Keralam over a generic drug used to treat the rare genetic condition. The concerns have brought questions about the safety, quality and effectiveness of medicines into focus. The discussion examines the importance of reliable information about treatment, regulatory oversight and the challenges families face in accessing medicines for rare diseases, where treatment costs can be a significant barrier.

The final segment revisits the history of Alzheimer’s disease through the case of Auguste Deter. In 1901, German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer began documenting the symptoms of Deter, a 51-year-old woman who experienced changes in memory, behaviour and her ability to carry out everyday activities. Her symptoms differed from cases he had typically encountered. After her death in 1906, Alzheimer examined her brain and identified changes that contributed to the understanding of the condition later named after him. The segment explores Deter’s experience and the role of clinical observation and patient documentation in the history of medical research.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

articles.title: KSSP supports distribution of generic drugs for SMA patients in Keralam
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) has supported the Kerala Health Department’s decision to provide a low-cost generic version of the drug Risdiplam to patients afflicted with Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare and threatening genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness.
In a statement, KSSP president C. Ramakrishnan and general secretary V. Manoj Kumar said that access to this medication is crucial for improving the quality of life and life expectancy of patients.
The statement from the pro-Left people’s science movement comes close on the heels of public health experts such as B. Ekbal, K.P. Aravindan, and V. Ramankutty endorsing the government’s stand.

The KSSP functionaries pointed out that Natco Pharma is an Indian pharmaceutical company that plays a key role in making affordable cancer treatments more accessible to the general public, both in India and in international markets. They claimed that the department’s decision is not merely aimed at saving public funds. It is a humanitarian responsibility to ensure that life-saving treatment is accessible to more SMA patients, they added.

articles.title: Farmers’ groups discuss list of demands ahead of meeting with Karnataka CM Shivakumar
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Nearly 30 leaders of various organisations discussed revising the minimum selling price for sugar and a higher Fair and Remunerative Price for sugarcane

Farmers’ groups on Sunday (October 25, 2026) attempted to reach a consensus on the list of demands to be presented ahead of a meeting with Karnataka Chief Minister D. K. Shivakumar in Belagavi on Monday (October 26, 2026).

Farmer leaders held a few meetings to prepare for the CM’s session. Some were skeptical about the outcome, and Union Food Minister Pralhad Joshi said he couldn’t attend, since the key demands involve the Central Government.

In Gurlapur, near the Belagavi–Bagalkot border, leaders Chunappa Pujeri and Shashikant Padasalagi spoke and then said they would call a Karnataka Bundh on Tuesday if the government doesn’t meet their demands.

“The CM told reporters in Bengaluru recently that he had extended an invitation to Mr. Joshi, but Joshi said he could not attend due to unavoidable circumstances, such as a pre-scheduled meeting in New Delhi. We are disappointed with Mr. Joshi. He should have cancelled all of his appointments and attended the Belagavi meeting,” said Chunappa Pujeri, a farmers’ leader.

Shashikant Padasalagi told reporters in Gurlapur on Sunday (October 25, 2026) that he would request the Chief Minister to switch the timing of his meetings. “Mr. Shivakumar has scheduled a meeting with factory owners in the morning and our meeting in the evening. He should ideally listen to us first and then direct the factories to fulfil our demands. He cannot first listen to the factories and then meet us,” he said.
Nearly 30 leaders of various organisations participated in an online meeting where the demands were discussed.

They listed several demands after the meeting, including Chukki Nanjundaswami, MLA Darshan Puttannaiah, Kuruburu Shantkumar, Badagalapura Nagendra, M. R. Veerappa, Siddarth Navi, and others. They discussed revising the minimum selling price for sugar and a higher Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) for sugarcane. The consensus was to urge the government to fix prices transparently, not rely on a “magic number.”

Most leaders argued that differential pricing for sugar—between domestic use and industry—should be their top priority. They claimed no legal changes were needed since the Union Government already provides LPC cylinders for different prices. Several also urged that all prices be treated as ex-field, with sugar mills bearing harvesting and transport costs.

Some leaders urged the Union Government to withdraw its decision not to procure sugarcane-based ethanol. Others urged implementing the C. Rangarajan committee’s recommendation to treat farmers as shareholders, not just suppliers. They pressed for a policy requiring factories to pay FRP for sugarcane and share profits from ethanol, co-generated power, molasses, and other byproducts.

Prof. Kammaradi asked the State Government to set up an open portal to document and monitor the activities of factories, including harvest, transport, payments to farmers, and recovery declarations. He said the State Government should take the lead in implementing the Rangarajan Committee report, as the UPA government at the Centre had appointed it.

Mr. Shantkumar said he would seek a State Advised Price, in addition to FRP, on the lines of Tamil Nadu. He said the government should act tough against factories that do not follow its pro-farmers decisions.

However, there were some differences. Some young farmers complained that there was a lack of unity among groups, especially among those from north and south Karnataka. Others did not agree with the demand that the State Government could act unilaterally to fix a SAP that would be remunerative, irrespective of the centrally fixed FRP.

articles.title: Launch of Garudan, smart bus punching system in Greater Kochi area, held up indefinitely
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The system was slated to be launched in August as a joint initiative of Kochi City Traffic Police and the Kochi City Bus Monitoring Committe

The launch of Garudan — an AI-ready smart bus punching, compliance monitoring and road-safety enforcement system in the Greater Kochi area has been indefinitely held up, due to delay in fine tuning technical issues and the bus operators allegedly being on different pages on mobilising funds to operate and maintain the system.

The smart punching system that was aimed at curbing reckless driving and over speeding by private buses in the city and its suburbs, was slated to be launched in August as a joint initiative of Kochi City Traffic Police and the Kochi City Bus Monitoring Committee. The body comprises of the operators of approximately 1,500 city and mofussil private buses that operate in the city, suburban towns and nearby districts.

“Under the project, a network of radio-frequency identification (RFID)-based smart bus-punching stations was to be readied at a dozen strategic locations in the Greater Kochi area, to digitally monitor bus operations, route compliance, and schedule adherence in real time. The real time punching by scanning of the QR code at each such station by bus crew, was to be compared to actual bus movements against approved schedules and operational parameters, enabling route-wise and bus-wise monitoring. This would help detect delays, early departures, missed punches, route violations, and the skipping of trips,” said a senior traffic police official who is associated with the initiative.

The smart punching stations project was to have RFID-based punching devices, surveillance support, server infrastructure, centralised monitoring dashboards and automated alerts. These were to provide digital evidence to the Kerala Police, the Motor Vehicles’ Department, the District Road Safety Council and the other agencies concerned. Its aim was to usher in improved reliability of public transport buses by adherence to time schedule and safe driving, while at the same time holding bus operators and crew accountable for unsafe driving practices and the unhealthy competition between buses, he added.
While the system was to be operated by the bus operators’ association, the police was to supervise it.

The secretary of the bus monitoring committee Navas K.M., who is also a bus owner, attributed the reckless driving by a section of bus operators to the withdrawal of time-punching cabins from different parts of the city about 15 years ago.

“In the proposed smart punching system, bus crew could either tap the QR code or swipe their card at the punching devices that would shortly be installed at Vyttila, Menaka, Kaloor, Ravipuram, Edapally, Kalamassery, Madavana, Vypin, Pettah, Thevara, Thopumpady and at Tripunithura,” he said.
In the proposed system, buses that arrived early at a punching station were to remit fine, it is learnt.

A bus operator attributed the delay in launching the system to a dispute over a sum of ₹3.8 lakh that remained in the account of the previous bus monitoring committee. “The balance ₹10 lakh needed for the project is expected to be raised as CSR funds. The amount is needed for the operation and maintenance of the smart punching units at the different locations.” he said.

articles.title: Meeshapulimala opens to tourists as Neelakurinji blooms
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: It is a rare occurrence as Neelakurinji usually does not bloom at such high altitudes

Meeshapulimala, one of the Munnar region’s highest peaks, is witnessing the blooming of Neelakurinji and will open to tourists starting Monday (October 26). The peak falls under the jurisdiction of the Kerala Forest Development Corporation (KFDC) in Munnar.

KFDC Munnar Manager Akhil Das said visitors will have the opportunity to view the blooms at higher elevations. “The KFDC has arranged multi-utility vehicles (MUVs) for the 30-kilometre journey from Munnar to Meeshapulimala at a fare of ₹1,250 per person. Tourists will be picked up from the Munnar KFDC office and transported in these specially arranged vehicles. The package includes a snack box and drinking water,” he said.

KFDC District Manager Sujith P.K. stated that the corporation, in association with the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI), has launched the ‘Kurinji’ mobile application for online bookings. Visitors can reserve slots and make payments directly through the app. “The key attraction at Meeshapulimala is the Neelakurinji bloom alongside sightings of the endangered Nilgiri tahr. KFDC plans to provide a unique ecotourism experience here,” Mr. Sujith said.

Officials added that the Kurinji mobile app lets users easily find locations and other travel details. Neelakurinji blooms were earlier witnessed at Chokramudy, under the Forest department, and at Korandakkad, under the KDHP tea estate. The two-month flowering season in those areas concluded recently. “Neelakurinji blooms typically progress from lower to higher elevations. Meeshapulimala, being at a higher altitude, experiences its peak flowering in October, which will last until December,” an official noted.
Neelakurinji in full bloom on the Meesapulimala hills. The KFDC has opened a Kurinji trek for enthusiasts to relish the spectacular sight. | Photo Credit: S. Anandan

Considering the environmental significance of the hills, authorities have capped the number of daily visitors at 750. “Apart from viewing the Neelakurinji blooms, tourists will also have the opportunity to trek the Meeshapulimala hills as part of the package,” an official said. The next Neelakurinji season in Munnar is expected to occur at the Eravikulam National Park in 2030. Devikulam Sub-Collector V.M. Arya officially inaugurated the Kurinji season at Meeshapulimala on Saturday.

Noted botanist Dr. Jomy Augustine said that Neelakurinji has finally bloomed in Meeshapulimala after prolonged concerns over delayed flowering. “Due to the El Niño effect and fluctuations in the monsoon, there were concerns that flowering might be aborted in the Meeshapulimala hills. However, the Kurinji has finally bloomed. We have been monitoring the flowering pattern on the hills over the past several days,” said Dr. Augustine.

​Dr. Augustine further noted that Neelakurinji does not normally bloom above 2,500 metres. “On the Anamudi hills in Munnar, there is no Neelakurinji bloom. However, in Meeshapulimala, the KFDC property Rhodo Mansion is situated at an elevation of 2,470 metres, and the Kurinji is blooming on the surrounding slopes. Considering these facts, the blooming in Meeshapulimala is very special,” he said.

articles.title: Srisailam temple to open three more laddu counters, including one for women, for Kartikam rush
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Trust Board chairman Pothugunta Ramesh Naidu inspects the queue lines, the Annaprasadam hall and the prasadam counters

Sri Bhramaramba Mallikarjuna Swamy temple Trust Board chairman Pothugunta Ramesh Naidu on Sunday (October 25, 2026) inspected the queue lines, the Annaprasadam (free meal) distribution hall and the laddu prasadam sales counters at Srisailam.

While examining the darshan queue lines and the holding compartments, Mr. Ramesh Naidu directed the officials concerned to take up necessary repairs to the flooring in the compartments. He interacted with several devotees to gather their feedback on the facilities provided by the Devasthanam, and inquired about the arrangements for darshan, supply of drinking water, distribution of prasadam and sanitation.

Mr. Ramesh Naidu instructed officials to identify areas where devotees might face difficulties during high footfall and to make appropriate arrangements accordingly. He stressed the need for precautions to prevent overcrowding or stampede-like situations in the queue lines and directed the staff concerned to remain in constant communication with their superiors while managing the darshan queues.

He asked officials to ensure a continuous supply of drinking water and refreshments in the queue lines. Information on darshan timings, the estimated time for darshan and other relevant details should be continuously broadcast through the temple’s public address system, he said.
He said special attention should be paid to the cleanliness of the restrooms in the queue complex and asked officials to ensure that they were cleaned regularly.

Inspecting the Annaprasadam distribution hall, Mr. Ramesh Naidu asked devotees about the food. Officials were advised to manage the distribution of Annaprasadam according to the expected influx of devotees during the auspicious month of Kartikam.
At the laddu prasadam sales counters, Mr. Ramesh Naidu reviewed the stock records and the procedure for issuing tickets.
He instructed the officials concerned to strictly maintain hygiene during the preparation of laddu and pulihora prasadams and said their quality must not be compromised.

Mr. Ramesh directed that adequate stock of laddus be kept ready to meet the requirements of the devotees. Officials were instructed to set up three additional laddu counters, including a dedicated counter for women, to accommodate the rush of devotees.
Staff were directed to ensure that devotees did not have to wait long at the prasadam sales counters.

articles.title: Bangladesh seeks details from Saudi Arabia on execution of two citizens: report
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The two Bangladesh nationals, a man and a woman, were executed on October 14, after being convicted of committing an “indecent act” inside a mosque in Makkah

Bangladesh has sought detailed information from Saudi Arabia about the execution of two of its citizens in the Makkah region, including the charges against them, court verdicts, manner of execution, whereabouts of their bodies and whether they had legal representation during their trials, according to a local media report.

The Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah sent a diplomatic letter to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs' branch in Makkah on October 19, seeking answers to six questions, according to a report by Bangladeshi newspaper Prothom Alo published on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
Bangladesh's Consul General in Jeddah also raised the matter with a senior Saudi foreign ministry official during a meeting the same day, the report said.
The two Bangladesh nationals, a man and a woman, were executed on October 14, after being convicted of committing an “indecent act” inside a mosque in Makkah.
The diplomatic letter seeks details of the offences, when and where they allegedly took place, the dates of arrest and certified copies of the court verdicts, the report said.

It also asks whether the death sentences were carried out by beheading or another method, where the bodies are being kept and whether they will be repatriated to Bangladesh or have already been buried in Saudi Arabia.
Bangladesh has also sought information on whether lawyers represented the two during the investigation and trial and whether they had requested legal assistance, the report said.

According to Prothom Alo , Bangladeshi officials said the country's missions did not have detailed information about the proceedings leading to the executions, including whether the two had legal representation.

A list of Bangladeshi prisoners shared by Saudi authorities in September reportedly contained allegations of adultery and an information technology-related offence involving the two, but did not specify their sentences.
Dhaka is seeking clarification on the discrepancy between those entries and the Saudi Interior Ministry's public explanation of the executions.
Bangladesh had also raised the executions with the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka, according to the Dhaka Tribune .

Bangladeshi officials said the government had not received detailed official information from Saudi authorities before learning that the executions had been carried out, the newspaper reported last week.

articles.title: Explosions heard in Saudi capital as airport prepares to reopen
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks
Explosions rang out in the Saudi capital on Sunday (October 25, 2026), as the kingdom was due to reopen Riyadh international airport despite repeated attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart, and has shifted the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war.
Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume on Sunday (October 25, 2026) after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.
However, it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.

The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the facility was still "unsafe" and a "military target".

"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional, and local airlines — as well as staff and travellers — against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."

An AFP journalist in the city heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday (October 25, 2026), with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards Riyadh, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.

articles.title: India advises its nationals in Saudi Arabia against filming missile interceptions
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The Indian mission also shared an update about the suspension of flights from Air India and Air India Express to and from Riyadh and Dammam

India on Sunday (October 25, 2026) advised its nationals in Saudi Arabia to abide by local rules and regulations and refrain from filming or publishing information related to missile and drone interceptions.
The advisory comes amid escalating tensions in the region due to a series of drone and missile attacks targeting civilian infrastructure by Yemen’s Houthis.

"The Indian community residing in Saudi Arabia is requested to abide by local rules and regulations," the Indian Embassy said on social media while reposting the notification issued by the Directorate of Saudi Civil Defence.
"Filming, publishing, or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability," the notification said.
The Indian mission also shared an update about the suspension of flights from Air India and Air India Express to and from Riyadh and Dammam.

"Air India and Air India Express flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam will remain suspended until 7 November 2026, while services to and from Jeddah will remain suspended until 31 October 2026," it posted on social media on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
The Consulate General of India in Jeddah also shared a similar advisory.

On Saturday (October 24, 2026), the Consulate General of India in Jeddah said its 24×7 Control Rooms in Jeddah and Makkah continued to provide necessary assistance to affected Indians, with support from community associations and volunteers.
The assistance includes food, essential medicines and other immediate requirements wherever needed and feasible, it said.

The mission also said it remained in regular contact with Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Hajj and Umrah and Ministry of Foreign Affairs to address difficulties caused by the flight disruptions, particularly issues concerning visa validity and delayed departures.
Meanwhile, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is preparing to resume domestic and international flight operations on Sunday, the Gulf News web portal reported.
It also quoted the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis as saying on Sunday that air defences had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh.

articles.title: Pakistan reopens Iran border crossing after week-long suspension of trade
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Resumption of operations in the Gabd-Rimdan crossing is expected to ease LPG shortage and reduce food and energy prices

Pakistan reopened a key border crossing with Iran to resume bilateral trade and cross-border movement after a week-long suspension that stranded freight vehicles, disrupted supplies and aggravated concerns over LPG shortage ahead of winter.

Trade operations resumed on Saturday (October 24, 2026) at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Balochistan's Gwadar district, with border officials allowing commercial consignments accompanied by consignment notes dated October 16 or earlier to cross, the Dawn newspaper reported.
Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, confirmed that the crossing, also known as Gate 250, has reopened.
"Pakistan has opened the border with Iran at Gabd-Rimdan... and allowed trucks and other vehicles to move toward Iran and Pakistan with import and export goods,” Mr. Kalmati said.

Welcoming the decision, he said the resumption of cross-border trade will bring immediate relief to traders and transporters stranded on both sides. He said the restored supply chain is expected to ease a nationwide LPG shortage and reduce soaring energy and food prices across Pakistan.

The reopening of the border comes days after Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir's visit to Iran earlier this week, during which he held talks with the Iranian leadership on bilateral relations and regional issues.

Pakistan's Commerce Ministry had closed the border and stopped cross-border movement on October 17. Though the Ministry did not specify a reason for the decision, the suspension was believed to be linked to security concerns.
The closure of the border had affected LPG supply in Pakistan, the demand for which rises with the onset of winter.

The suspension was followed by an attack on freight vehicles stranded near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing. On Thursday (October 22, 2026), unidentified gunmen targeted the parked trucks, setting dozens ablaze and damaging several others.
The reopening on Saturday (October 24, 2026) followed a review of the security situation by local administrators, who deployed additional forces to protect trade convoys.

Pakistan and Iran share a 909-km border that separates Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan province from Pakistan's Balochistan province. The border crossings serve as important routes for bilateral commerce and the movement of goods in the region.
